title: How does a neuron fire?
question: How does a neuron decide to fire, and what happens after it does?
representation: A QWEEPS-planned mechanism: resting battery, summed inputs at the hillock, threshold decision, Na+ upstroke, fixed spike shape, self-regenerating propagation, and reset with transmitter hand-off. Native ManimGL beats carry the mechanism; layout beats isolate the summation, all-or-none shape, and molecular reset.

example.title: A hot-mug touch
example.description: Follow one sensory axon from the receptor to the next cell.

chapters.title: A charged battery at rest
chapters.question: What is ready to fire before anything happens?
chapters.insight: At rest the inside is about -70 mV because Na+ is kept outside, K+ inside, and open K+ leak plus pumps hold the imbalance.
chapters.narration: At rest, the inside of the neuron sits near minus seventy millivolts. Sodium is kept outside, potassium inside; leak channels and pumps hold that imbalance, so the membrane is a charged battery waiting to be disturbed.

roles.membrane: Membrane: the boundary that separates inside from outside.
roles.ions: Ion gradients: Na+ outside, K+ inside.
roles.pumps: Leak channels and the Na+/K+ pump hold the standing gradient.

cues.text: At rest the inside is negative and the outside is positive.
Na+ outside and K+ inside form a stored battery.

nodes.title: Membrane
nodes.body: A lipid bilayer separating inside from outside.

nodes.title: Ion gradients
nodes.body: Na+ outside, K+ inside: a stored battery.

nodes.title: Leak + pumps
nodes.body: Leak channels and the Na+/K+ pump hold the gradient.

visual.takeaway: At rest the membrane is a charged battery: Na+ outside, K+ inside, held by leaks and pumps.

presentation.why: The resting gradient is the state every later change alters.
presentation.visualEvidence: The membrane, ion dots and voltage meter assemble into a stable -70 mV battery.

continuity.bridge: Opening beat: establish the resting battery before anything changes.

chapters.title: Many whispers, one decision point
chapters.question: How does the neuron combine incoming nudges?
chapters.insight: Small graded EPSPs and IPSPs flow to the axon hillock and add up; only their sum decides what happens next.
chapters.narration: Inputs arrive as small graded voltages. Excitatory inputs push the hillock up, inhibitory inputs pull it down; the neuron adds them, and only their sum at the axon hillock matters.

roles.epsp: Excitatory input: pushes the hillock voltage up.
roles.ipsp: Inhibitory input: pulls the hillock voltage down.
roles.hillock: Axon hillock: sums the inputs and decides whether to fire.

cues.text: Excitatory and inhibitory inputs add at the hillock.

nodes.title: Excitatory input
nodes.body: A small depolarising nudge from a synapse.

nodes.title: Inhibitory input
nodes.body: A small hyperpolarising nudge from another synapse.

nodes.title: Axon hillock
nodes.body: Where the summed voltage is read and the decision is made.

visual.takeaway: Only the summed voltage at the hillock decides what happens next.

presentation.why: The decision is a sum of opposing inputs, not a single synapse.
presentation.visualEvidence: Excitatory and inhibitory nudges converge on one hillock; their signs add.

continuity.bridge: The battery is established; now see how it is nudged.

chapters.title: Threshold: fire or stay silent
chapters.question: Why do small nudges fade but a big enough push fires?
chapters.insight: Below about -55 mV charge leaks away; above it voltage-gated channels open and the response becomes all-or-none.
chapters.narration: Below about minus fifty-five millivolts the charge leaks away and nothing happens. Cross that threshold, and voltage-gated sodium channels open; the response becomes all-or-none.

roles.small: Small push: a depolarisation that stays below threshold.
roles.threshold: Threshold: about -55 mV at the hillock.
roles.big: Suprathreshold push: opens voltage-gated Na+ channels and fires.

cues.text: A small push decays below threshold.
Crossing -55 mV opens the voltage-gated gates.

nodes.title: Small push
nodes.body: The summed voltage stays below -55 mV.

nodes.title: Threshold -55 mV
nodes.body: The decision line at the axon hillock.

nodes.title: Crossing it
nodes.body: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open; firing becomes all-or-none.

visual.takeaway: Below threshold the charge leaks away; above it the response becomes all-or-none.

presentation.why: The threshold is the decision boundary the learner must see.
presentation.visualEvidence: Two pushes of different size are applied at the hillock; one decays, one opens the gates.

continuity.bridge: The summed voltage is read against one boundary.

chapters.title: The flood that is the spike
chapters.question: What actually makes voltage shoot up?
chapters.insight: Crossing threshold opens voltage-gated Na+ channels; Na+ rush in and positive feedback drives the rise to about +30 mV.
chapters.narration: Open sodium channels let sodium rush in. That makes the inside more positive, which opens more channels — positive feedback drives the spike toward plus thirty millivolts.

roles.gates: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open at threshold.
roles.flood: Na+ influx: positive charge enters the cell.
roles.feedback: Positive feedback: depolarisation opens more channels.

cues.text: Na+ enters and drives the inside positive.

nodes.title: Open Na+ gates
nodes.body: Voltage-gated channels open at threshold.

nodes.title: Na+ influx
nodes.body: Sodium enters and makes the inside positive.

nodes.title: Positive feedback
nodes.body: More depolarisation opens more channels.

visual.takeaway: Threshold opens Na+ gates; the influx drives a positive-feedback rise to +30 mV.

presentation.why: The upstroke is a feedback loop, not a passive leak.
presentation.visualEvidence: Na+ dots cross the membrane through open gates and the voltage meter rises.

continuity.bridge: The threshold has been crossed; now follow the positive-feedback flood.

chapters.title: How high, how fast, how brief
chapters.question: What shape is the spike in time?
chapters.insight: The spike lasts ~1-2 ms with fixed height; a bigger touch does not make a bigger spike, only more spikes.
chapters.narration: The spike is brief and fixed in height: about one to two milliseconds, the same size each time. A stronger touch does not make a taller spike; it makes more spikes.

roles.strong: Stronger input: additional spikes, not a taller one.

cues.text: The spike rises and falls in about 1-2 ms.
A stronger touch adds spikes, not height.

nodes.title: Just at threshold
nodes.body: One spike: the same height and duration as any other.

nodes.title: Well above threshold
nodes.body: A stronger touch produces more spikes, not a taller one.

visual.takeaway: The spike is all-or-none in height; stronger input changes the number of spikes, not their size.

presentation.why: All-or-none is easiest to see when two inputs are compared on the same trace.
presentation.visualEvidence: Two traces have equal peak height and width; only the spike count differs.

continuity.bridge: The flood has a characteristic shape in time.

chapters.title: The wave that recharges itself
chapters.question: How does the spike travel without fading?
chapters.insight: Local current depolarises the next patch to threshold, so each segment regenerates the spike toward the terminals.
chapters.narration: The spike does not fade as it travels. Local current depolarises the next patch of membrane to threshold, so each segment regenerates the signal down the axon.

roles.zone: Active zone: the membrane segment currently firing.
roles.next: Next patch: depolarised by local current to threshold.
roles.terminal: Axon terminals: the signal arrives undiminished.

cues.text: The active zone is only a small patch at a time.
Each patch regenerates the spike for the next.

nodes.title: Active zone
nodes.body: The patch of membrane currently above threshold.

nodes.title: Next patch
nodes.body: Local current pushes the next segment to threshold.

nodes.title: Terminals
nodes.body: The signal arrives without fading.

visual.takeaway: Each segment regenerates the spike, so the signal reaches the terminals undiminished.

presentation.why: Propagation is repeated regeneration, not a passive cable.
presentation.visualEvidence: A bright active zone moves along the axon and lights successive patches.

continuity.bridge: A single spike has a fixed shape; now see how that shape moves.

chapters.title: Reset and hand-off
chapters.question: How does the neuron reset and talk to the next cell?
chapters.insight: K+ exit repolarises, the refractory period blocks re-firing, pumps restore gradients, and Ca2+ triggers transmitter release.
chapters.narration: Potassium leaving repolarises the membrane, the refractory period prevents immediate re-firing, and the sodium-potassium pump restores the gradients. At the terminals, calcium triggers vesicles to hand the signal to the next cell.

roles.pump: Na+/K+ pump: restores the ion gradients.

cues.text: K+ exit brings the voltage back down.
Pumps restore Na+ and K+ gradients.
Calcium triggers transmitter release to the next cell.

nodes.title: K+ leaves
nodes.body: Potassium exit repolarises the membrane.

nodes.title: Pumps restore
nodes.body: The Na+/K+ pump swaps ions back to their gradients.

nodes.title: Ca2+ enters
nodes.body: Calcium at the terminal triggers vesicle fusion.

nodes.title: Next cell
nodes.body: Transmitter hands the signal to the next neuron.

visual.takeaway: Repolarisation, pumping and calcium release reset the neuron and pass the signal on.

presentation.why: Reset and transmission are a sequence with distinct molecular steps.
presentation.visualEvidence: K+ exit, pump restoration, calcium entry and vesicle release follow one another.

continuity.bridge: The signal has arrived; now the neuron must reset and pass it on.
